## Reporting a problem

`birdnet_sitrep()` shows which Python environment birdnetR uses:

```{r}
birdnet_sitrep()
#> python_version: 3.12.14
#> python_executable: /home/user/.cache/uv/archive-v0/0MLD8yprGexELXHg/bin/python
#> birdnet_version: 1.4.0
#> runtimes: onnxruntime, ai_edge_litert
```

- `python_version`, `python_executable`: the Python that birdnetR runs on.
- `birdnet_version`: the version of the `birdnet` Python package.
- `runtimes`: the installed inference runtimes, out of `onnxruntime`,
  `ai_edge_litert` (LiteRT), `tensorflow` and `torch`.

Please include this output when you
[report a bug](https://github.com/birdnet-team/birdnetR/issues).

After birdnetR has installed TensorFlow or PyTorch during a session (see
[Extra downloads](#extra-downloads)), `python_executable` points to a different
folder than before. That is expected: reticulate adds the new packages as an
extra layer on top of the existing environment.


## Long pause after prediction

If you notice a long pause after BirdNET has finished processing your audio but before you get the results, this is likely the conversion from Python to R in `as.data.frame()`. This is particularly noticeable when:

- processing long audio files (> 20 minutes),
- using low confidence thresholds that generate many predictions (`min_confidence < 0.1`),
- working with little memory.

### Solution: use `birdnet_write()`

For large results, use `birdnet_write()` to write them directly from Python to a file (CSV, Parquet, or NumPy) without converting them to an R data frame first.

```{r}
model <- birdnet_load()
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, audio_path)

# Write directly from Python - no R conversion needed
birdnet_write(predictions, "results.csv")
```

For tips on processing many files, see the
[workflow](workflow.html) article.


## Parallel processing

Don't run birdnetR inside `parallel` or `future` workers (for example with
`parallel::parLapply()`, `future.apply::future_lapply()` or `furrr`). Each
worker is a fresh R session without birdnetR's Python setup, so birdnet does
not work reliably there (see
[#56](https://github.com/birdnet-team/birdnetR/issues/56)).

`birdnet_predict()` and `birdnet_encode()` already run in parallel. Pass all
files in one call and set the number of parallel workers with `n_workers`:

```{r}
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, n_workers = 8L)
```


## Extra downloads

The default installation contains ONNX Runtime and LiteRT. It runs BirdNET+
V3.0 and BirdNET V2.4 models, and custom TFLite classifiers trained on V2.4.
Some models need more:

| You load | birdnetR installs | Download |
|---|---|---|
| `birdnet_load_perch()` | TensorFlow | about 600 MB |
| `birdnet_load(backend = "pb")`, Raven exports | TensorFlow | about 600 MB |
| `backend = "tf"` with `library = "tflite"`, or where LiteRT is not available (Intel Macs, Windows on ARM) | TensorFlow | about 600 MB |
| `birdnet_load(backend = "pt")` | PyTorch | several GB with GPU support, much less for the CPU-only version |

birdnetR installs these the first time you load such a model, also in the
middle of an R session. That one load takes longer. `birdnet_list_models()`
shows in its `needs` column which models need what.

### Intel Macs

On Intel Macs, TensorFlow can only be added before Python starts. If you load
a model that needs TensorFlow after Python has started (for example after
loading another model), birdnetR stops with:

```
On Intel Macs, TensorFlow must be added before Python starts. Restart R and make this load your first birdnetR call.
```

Restart R and load the TensorFlow model first. Perch v2 does not run on Intel
Macs at all.

### Your own Python environment

If you set `RETICULATE_PYTHON` to the Python of your own virtual environment,
birdnetR uses that environment and does not change it. It also can't install
the extras there. Install them yourself, for example with
`reticulate::virtualenv_install("my-env", "birdnet[tf]")` for TensorFlow or
`"birdnet[pt]"` for PyTorch. If a runtime is missing, the `birdnet` Python
package stops with an error that names it.

`RETICULATE_PYTHON` must be set before Python starts: in your `.Renviron` file,
or with `Sys.setenv()` before you load the first model. Note that
`reticulate::use_virtualenv()` alone does not work with birdnetR: birdnetR sets
`RETICULATE_PYTHON` to reticulate's managed environment when it is unset, and
`RETICULATE_PYTHON` takes precedence.


## Working offline

Models are downloaded the first time you load them. Run your analysis once
while online, so that Python, the Python packages and the models are on disk.

Releases of the `birdnet` Python package newer than 1.4.0 never try to
download anything when the environment variable `BIRDNET_OFFLINE` is `1`. Set
it before you load a model:

```{r}
Sys.setenv(BIRDNET_OFFLINE = "1")
model <- birdnet_load()
```


## Harmless console messages

- Decoding MP3 files (for example the bundled `soundscape.mp3`) can print
  libmpg123 errors such as `part2_3_length ... too large`. The results are not
  affected.
- TensorFlow prints CUDA or XLA log lines on computers without an NVIDIA GPU,
  for example `failed call to cuInit`. You can ignore them.


## GPU

By default, all models run on the CPU. A GPU can speed up very large
analyses.

Not every backend can use a GPU:

- `"pt"` (PyTorch, BirdNET+ V3.0 only) and `"pb"` (TensorFlow, all models
  including Perch v2) can.
- `"onnx"` can, but only in a Python environment you set up yourself (see
  [ONNX Runtime](#onnx-runtime-bring-your-own-environment)).
- `"tf"` (TensorFlow Lite) runs on the CPU only.

`birdnet_use_gpu()` declares the Python packages for GPU support. Call it at
the top of your script, before you load any model, because the packages are
resolved when Python starts. Choose one backend per R session: TensorFlow and
PyTorch each bring their own CUDA libraries, which can conflict.

Then pass `device = "GPU"` when you predict or encode. If something does not
work, restart R without `birdnet_use_gpu()` to go back to the CPU.

### Linux with an NVIDIA GPU: PyTorch

```{r}
birdnet_use_gpu("pt")
model <- birdnet_load(backend = "pt")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")
```

This installs `birdnet[pt]`. If the environment variable `UV_TORCH_BACKEND` is
not set, birdnetR sets it to `"auto"`, so the installer picks the PyTorch build
that matches your GPU driver. The NVIDIA driver must be installed.

### Linux with an NVIDIA GPU: TensorFlow

```{r}
birdnet_use_gpu("pb")
model <- birdnet_load(backend = "pb")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")

# Perch v2
perch <- birdnet_load_perch(device = "GPU")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(perch, files, device = "GPU")
```

This installs `birdnet[and-cuda]`, TensorFlow with its CUDA libraries. The
NVIDIA driver and CUDA must already be installed on your system.

### Linux with an AMD GPU (ROCm, experimental)

PyTorch has builds for AMD GPUs (ROCm). Tell the installer which one to use
before calling `birdnet_use_gpu()`:

```{r}
Sys.setenv(UV_TORCH_BACKEND = "rocm6.4")
birdnet_use_gpu("pt")
model <- birdnet_load(backend = "pt")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")
```

Use the newest `rocmX.Y` value that matches the ROCm version installed on your
system. Older values can resolve to an old PyTorch release. ROCm support is
experimental: not every AMD GPU is supported by ROCm.

### macOS with Apple silicon: TensorFlow with Metal

```{r}
birdnet_use_gpu("pb")
model <- birdnet_load(backend = "pb")
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")
```

This installs `birdnet[tf]` and `tensorflow-metal`, Apple's GPU plugin for
TensorFlow. Two caveats:

- The `birdnet` Python package lists GPU use of the Protobuf (`"pb"`) backend
  on macOS as unsupported.
- `tensorflow-metal` is often released later than TensorFlow, so the newest
  TensorFlow may not work with it yet.

### ONNX Runtime: bring your own environment

The GPU version of ONNX Runtime (`onnxruntime-gpu`) has to replace the regular
`onnxruntime`, which the `birdnet` package depends on. birdnetR can't do that
in its managed environment, so you create your own environment once. You need
an NVIDIA GPU with the CUDA and cuDNN versions that
[ONNX Runtime requires](https://onnxruntime.ai/docs/execution-providers/CUDA-ExecutionProvider.html#requirements).

```{r}
# Once: create a virtual environment with birdnet and onnxruntime-gpu.
# It needs Python 3.11 to 3.13 on your system (see reticulate::install_python()).
reticulate::virtualenv_create("birdnet-gpu", version = "3.12")
reticulate::virtualenv_install("birdnet-gpu", "birdnet>=1.4,<2")
reticulate::virtualenv_remove("birdnet-gpu", packages = "onnxruntime", confirm = FALSE)
reticulate::virtualenv_install("birdnet-gpu", "onnxruntime-gpu")
```

In every session, point `RETICULATE_PYTHON` at this environment before you
load the first model (or set it in your `.Renviron` file):

```{r}
Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = reticulate::virtualenv_python("birdnet-gpu"))
library(birdnetR)

model <- birdnet_load()
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files, device = "GPU")
```

If you later upgrade `birdnet` in this environment, check that
`onnxruntime` did not come back, and remove it again. Extras such as TensorFlow
are not installed automatically in your own environment (see
[Your own Python environment](#your-own-python-environment)).

### Other platforms

On other platforms, for example Windows, `birdnet_use_gpu()` stops with an
error because there is no automatic setup. You can build your own environment
as in the ONNX Runtime section.
